stem: An organization reports 99% completion for annual phishing awareness training, but simulated-phishing results show the same high-risk departments continue to submit credentials at nearly the same rate. What is the BEST next step for the awareness program?
decision_point: measure and improve behavior rather than treating course completion as the primary success metric
misconceptions: completion rate alone proves awareness effectiveness
repeating the same annual course is always the best remediation
training should be identical for every role regardless of risk

originality.authoring_note: Original awareness-effectiveness scenario distinguishing course completion from persistent phishing behavior.

options: Use the simulation and incident data to identify the risky behaviors and populations, provide targeted reinforcement or role-relevant exercises, and track whether measurable behavior improves over time
Keep the existing course unchanged because a 99% completion rate proves the program is effective
Stop simulations because users who fail them may become discouraged
Require every employee to take the same course twice per year without changing content or measurement
explanation: Awareness effectiveness should be judged by whether risky behavior and outcomes improve, not merely whether users completed training. Targeted, role-relevant reinforcement and repeated behavioral measurement directly address the observed gap.
distractor_rationales: Awareness effectiveness should be judged by whether risky behavior and outcomes improve, not merely whether users completed training. Targeted, role-relevant reinforcement and repeated behavioral measurement directly address the observed gap.
Completion is an activity metric; persistent unsafe behavior shows that completion alone is not adequate evidence of effectiveness.
Well-designed simulations can provide useful behavioral evidence and learning opportunities when used ethically and constructively.
Repeating unchanged content for everyone does not address the demonstrated difference in risk or prove that behavior will improve.

stem: A company must prove that an executive approved a high-value transaction and that the approval message was not altered afterward. Confidentiality of the approval text is not required. Which control BEST supports the needed security properties?
decision_point: select a control that provides integrity and origin authentication with evidence that can support nonrepudiation
misconceptions: encryption is required whenever integrity is needed
hashing alone proves who approved a message
a digital signature automatically provides confidentiality

originality.authoring_note: Original security-properties scenario choosing origin/tamper evidence without a confidentiality requirement.

options: Encrypt the message with a shared symmetric key and discard all signer identity records
Use a properly managed digital-signature process tied to the executive’s verified identity and protected private key, retaining verification evidence
Store only an unkeyed hash of the message with no authenticated association to the executive
Compress the approval message and send it over a private network
explanation: A properly implemented digital signature can provide integrity and origin authentication and can support nonrepudiation when identity, private-key control, certificate or key validity, and verification evidence are trustworthy. It does not require confidentiality of the signed content.
distractor_rationales: Shared-key encryption can provide confidentiality and sometimes integrity when used in an authenticated construction, but shared secrets do not provide the same signer-specific evidence and are unnecessary when confidentiality is not required.

A properly implemented digital signature can provide integrity and origin authentication and can support nonrepudiation when identity, private-key control, certificate or key validity, and verification evidence are trustworthy. It does not require confidentiality of the signed content.
A hash can show whether content changed when a trusted reference exists, but by itself it does not authenticate which executive approved the message.
Compression and private-network placement do not provide cryptographic proof of origin or tamper evidence.

stem: A cloud application is being retired after its functions move to a new platform. The project manager plans to delete the user interface and close the project, but old API credentials, service accounts, replicated data, monitoring integrations, and DNS entries would remain active. Which retirement approach is BEST?
decision_point: carry security assurance through retirement by removing residual access, data, dependencies, and operational references
misconceptions: removing the user interface completes secure retirement
unused service accounts are harmless if undocumented
retirement controls are only an asset-disposal concern

originality.authoring_note: Original lifecycle-retirement scenario focused on residual cloud identities, data, and integrations after functional migration.

options: Delete the user interface and leave all back-end integrations in place in case the application is needed later
Disable monitoring first so retirement alerts do not delay project closure

Execute a verified retirement plan that revokes credentials and service accounts, removes or migrates data according to retention rules, disables interfaces and dependencies, updates inventories and DNS, and confirms residual access paths are closed
Keep the old application reachable but undocumented because obscurity reduces the chance of attack
explanation: Security assurance extends through system retirement. A complete retirement removes or transfers residual data, identities, interfaces, integrations, and inventory references and verifies that obsolete access paths and dependencies no longer remain active.
distractor_rationales: The application can remain exploitable through back-end identities, APIs, data, or integrations even when its visible interface is removed.
Monitoring should support safe retirement and verification; disabling it first can remove evidence needed to confirm that residual activity has stopped.

Security assurance extends through system retirement. A complete retirement removes or transfers residual data, identities, interfaces, integrations, and inventory references and verifies that obsolete access paths and dependencies no longer remain active.
Undocumented systems are harder to govern and patch and remain exposed despite being less visible to administrators.

stem: A new industrial monitoring system must remain available during a single-site outage, protect regulated telemetry from unauthorized disclosure, and restrict administrative actions to a small set of highly trusted operators. The architecture team starts by copying every control from a generic baseline before documenting these requirements or the system’s threat context. What is the BEST correction?
subtopics: derive controls from system security requirements
decision_point: derive and tailor controls from explicit availability confidentiality administrative-assurance requirements and threat context before finalizing the control set
misconceptions: a generic baseline is sufficient without system context
all controls should be implemented before requirements are known
control selection should be driven only by technology preference

originality.authoring_note: Original control-selection scenario using mixed availability, confidentiality, and administrative-assurance requirements in an industrial context.

options: Keep the copied baseline unchanged because generic baselines already represent the final risk decision
Choose controls only according to which products the operations team already owns
Delay security requirements until after deployment so actual incidents reveal which controls were necessary

Document and analyze the system security requirements, architecture, dependencies, and threat context, then select and tailor a control set that provides the required assurance and validate it against those requirements
explanation: Baselines can be useful starting points, but final control selection should be derived and tailored from explicit system security requirements, architecture, dependencies, threat context, and assurance needs. Validation should then show that the selected controls satisfy those requirements.
distractor_rationales: A generic baseline cannot by itself account for the system’s specific mission, architecture, availability needs, regulated data, or privileged-access risks.
Existing products can influence implementation feasibility but should not define the security requirements or final control set by themselves.
Waiting for incidents to establish requirements is reactive and can leave predictable risks unaddressed during design and deployment.

Baselines can be useful starting points, but final control selection should be derived and tailored from explicit system security requirements, architecture, dependencies, threat context, and assurance needs. Validation should then show that the selected controls satisfy those requirements.
